name: Corona Spiral

detectability.signature: Broadband electromagnetic emission with cyclical intensity peaks and rotating polarization vector

proximity: Electromagnetic interference disrupts unshielded communications and sensor arrays
Static charge accumulates on hull surfaces, causing sporadic arcing between components
Navigation instruments fluctuate in time with the vortex rotation cycle
contact: Unshielded electronics are overloaded and destroyed within seconds
Hull plating absorbs enormous thermal energy, exceeding radiator capacity on most vessels
Crew experience painful static discharge and sensory overstimulation from ambient energy
prolonged_exposure: Cumulative electromagnetic damage renders all onboard systems inoperable
Hull integrity compromised as thermal stress fractures propagate through superstructure
Radiation exposure reaches lethal thresholds even behind standard shielding

age: Approximately 80 million years, predating the formation of the nearest stellar system

behavior.cycle: Primary rotation completes every 7.3 standard hours; intensity peaks every 22 hours

phenomena: Vast arms of luminous plasma sweep outward from the center in a slow, hypnotic spiral visible across light-years
The vortex emits harmonic electromagnetic frequencies that can be converted to audio — a deep, resonant drone that rises and falls with the rotation
Smaller secondary eddies form and collapse at the spiral's edges, briefly reaching temperatures comparable to stellar coronae
Charged particle streams trace the magnetic field lines in brilliant filaments of blue-white light
hazards: The spiral arms sweep through surrounding space unpredictably, extending the danger zone during intensity peaks
Secondary eddies can form outside the predicted boundary, trapping vessels that believed they were at safe distance
Electromagnetic pulses during peak cycles can disable ships up to 50,000 km from the visible boundary
opportunities: Energy harvesting stations positioned at calculated safe distances can capture enormous power during peak cycles
The vortex interior contains plasma in exotic states useful for advanced materials research
The harmonic emissions carry information about deep-space magnetic field structures otherwise unmeasurable
known_incidents: The energy harvesting platform Daybreak Array operated profitably for eleven years before a peak cycle 40% above predicted intensity destroyed it in 2241, killing its crew of thirty-two
A racing pilot named Vel Surenne famously skimmed the outer spiral arm on a dare in 2267, surviving with a fused navigation console and permanent hearing damage from the electromagnetic resonance
description: Corona Spiral is a vast whirlpool of luminous energy turning slowly in the void, its arms of superheated plasma stretching thousands of kilometers outward in a display visible to the naked eye from neighboring systems. The center burns white-hot, a knot of electromagnetic fury that has been spinning since before the nearest stars ignited. At its edges, the arms fade into delicate filaments of charged particles tracing invisible magnetic architecture in threads of pale blue light.

The vortex rotates on a predictable cycle, but its intensity fluctuates in ways that resist precise modeling. Every twenty-two hours, the spiral flares — its arms extending further, its emissions spiking across the electromagnetic spectrum, its secondary eddies spawning and dying in bursts of coronal fire. Ships maintaining safe distance during calm periods can find themselves engulfed when a peak cycle pushes the boundary outward. The energy is staggering; a single peak cycle releases more power than most civilizations consume in a year.

Corona Spiral has been a navigational landmark and scientific curiosity since its discovery by the Farwatch Observatory network in the early colonial period. Its origin remains debated — some astrophysicists argue it is the remnant of a stellar collision, others that it represents a self-sustaining magnetic dynamo with no precedent in known physics. The destruction of Daybreak Array tempered commercial enthusiasm, but research interest has only grown as new instruments reveal deeper structure within the vortex.

The Spiral continues to turn, indifferent to observation and exploitation alike. Current monitoring satellites track its cycles with reasonable accuracy, though the margin of error on peak intensity predictions remains uncomfortably wide. Three separate consortiums are designing next-generation harvesting platforms with improved safety margins, each racing to tap the anomaly's potential. Navigators treat it with wary respect — beautiful from a distance, merciless up close, and always, always spinning.
